title_th: การสั่งอาหารที่ร้าน
register: Casual-polite (friendly service register: first names not used, but 'please', 'thanks', 'sorry' carry the politeness — not grammar formality)

targets.why_it_matters_here: The whole order lives in the last sound. Drop the /d/ and /s/ and 'fried rice' becomes 'fry rye'; 'no ice' becomes 'no eye'; 'the bill' becomes 'the bin'. A vanished final consonant here means the wrong plate arrives — and you still pay for it.

'Three people' heard as 'tree people' gets you the wrong table, and 'three coffees' heard as 'tree coffees' gets you the wrong bill. 'Thanks' and 'that's' are the two lines you say most in a meal — if they sound like 'tanks' and 'dat's', every turn starts with a repair.

model_dialogues.label: A2 — A straightforward dinner order (scripted, everything goes to plan)

lines.speaker: Server
lines.text: Hi there! Table for how many?
lines.th: สวัสดีค่ะ! กี่ท่านคะ?

lines.speaker: Customer
lines.text: Three people, please.
lines.th: สามคนครับ

lines.speaker: Server
lines.text: Right this way. Here's the menu.
lines.th: เชิญทางนี้เลยค่ะ นี่เมนูค่ะ

lines.speaker: Server
lines.text: Are you ready to order?
lines.th: พร้อมสั่งหรือยังคะ?

lines.speaker: Customer
lines.text: Yes. I'd like the chicken curry.
lines.th: พร้อมแล้วครับ ขอแกงกะหรี่ไก่

lines.speaker: Server
lines.text: Sure. Anything to drink?
lines.th: ได้ค่ะ รับเครื่องดื่มอะไรไหมคะ?

lines.speaker: Customer
lines.text: Just water. No ice, thanks.
lines.th: เอาน้ำเปล่าพอ ไม่ใส่น้ำแข็งนะครับ

lines.speaker: Customer
lines.text: And what do you recommend for dessert?
lines.th: แล้วของหวานมีอะไรแนะนำบ้างครับ?

lines.speaker: Server
lines.text: The mango cheesecake is really good.
lines.th: ชีสเค้กมะม่วงอร่อยมากค่ะ

lines.speaker: Customer (after the meal)
lines.text: Excuse me — could we get the bill?
lines.th: ขอโทษครับ — ขอบิลหน่อยได้ไหมครับ?

model_dialogues.label: B1 — Same restaurant, three things go wrong (sold out, allergy check, wrong dish)

lines.speaker: Server
lines.text: Evening! Just the two of you?
lines.th: สวัสดีตอนเย็นค่ะ! สองท่านใช่ไหมคะ?

lines.speaker: Customer
lines.text: Yes, two please.
lines.th: ใช่ครับ สองคน

lines.speaker: Server
lines.text: You're in luck — there's a table by the window. Here's the menu.
lines.th: โชคดีนะคะ พอดีมีโต๊ะริมหน้าต่างว่าง นี่เมนูค่ะ

lines.speaker: Customer
lines.text: Thanks. Could we get two waters?
lines.th: ขอบคุณครับ ขอน้ำเปล่าสองแก้วได้ไหมครับ?

lines.speaker: Server
lines.text: Sparkling or still?
lines.th: เอาแบบมีฟอง (sparkling) หรือน้ำเปล่าธรรมดาคะ?

lines.speaker: Customer
lines.text: Still, thanks.
lines.th: ธรรมดาครับ ขอบคุณ

lines.speaker: Server
lines.text: No worries. Ready to order, or do you need a minute?
lines.th: ได้เลยค่ะ พร้อมสั่งเลยไหม หรือขอเวลาดูเมนูอีกสักครู่คะ?

lines.speaker: Customer
lines.text: We're ready. I'd like the grilled fish.
lines.th: พร้อมแล้วครับ ขอปลาย่าง

lines.speaker: Server
lines.text: Ah, sorry — the fish is off tonight. We've sold out.
lines.th: อุ๊ย ขอโทษด้วยค่ะ — คืนนี้ปลาหมดแล้วค่ะ

lines.speaker: Customer
lines.text: Oh. What do you recommend instead?
lines.th: อ้าว งั้นมีอะไรแนะนำแทนไหมครับ?

lines.speaker: Server
lines.text: The lamb's popular, or the mushroom risotto if you want something lighter.

lines.speaker: Customer
lines.text: I'll take the risotto. Does it have peanuts?

lines.speaker: Server
lines.text: No peanuts, but there's cream in it. Any allergies I should know about?

lines.speaker: Customer
lines.text: I'm allergic to shellfish.
lines.th: ผมแพ้อาหารทะเลพวกกุ้งหอยปูครับ

lines.text: Here we are — one lamb.
lines.th: นี่ค่ะ — เนื้อแกะหนึ่งที่

lines.speaker: Customer
lines.text: Sorry, I think that's not mine. I ordered the risotto.
lines.th: ขอโทษครับ อันนี้ไม่ใช่ของผมนะ ผมสั่งริซอตโต้ครับ

lines.text: Oh, my mistake. I'll fix that right now.

lines.text: Thanks. Could we get separate bills after?
lines.th: ขอบคุณครับ แล้วเดี๋ยวขอแยกบิลได้ไหมครับ?

lines.text: Of course. Back in a moment.
lines.th: ได้เลยค่ะ สักครู่นะคะ

chunk_drills.label: Ordering politely — the safe opener
examples: I'd like the fried rice, please.
I'd like a coffee, no sugar.
chunk_drills.spiralled_grammar: 'would like' as a fixed polite chunk (recycled from shopping) — never taught as conditional grammar; contrast with the blunt 'I want'.

chunk_drills.label: Asking for things at the table
chunk_drills.pattern: Could we get ___, please? / Could I have ___?
examples: Could we get two waters, please?
chunk_drills.spiralled_grammar: 'could' for requests (recycled from phone/service units); final /d/ + /t/ cluster in 'could we get' is the pronunciation load.

chunk_drills.label: Getting help choosing
chunk_drills.pattern: What do you recommend? / Which one is ___? / Is the ___ spicy?
chunk_drills.spiralled_grammar: Wh- questions with 'do' + comparative adjectives (recycled from shopping comparisons).

chunk_drills.label: Food safety — allergies and ingredients
chunk_drills.pattern: Does it have ___ in it? / I'm allergic to ___. / No ___, please.
examples: Does it have peanuts in it?
Does this have fish sauce in it?
No salt on the fries, please.
chunk_drills.spiralled_grammar: 'Does it have…?' present-simple question with 'do' support; 'be allergic to + noun' as a fixed safety chunk.

chunk_drills.label: Soft complaining — fixing a problem without a fight
chunk_drills.pattern: Sorry, I think ___. / This isn't what I ordered.
examples: Sorry, I think that's not mine.
Sorry, I think this is the wrong one.
Sorry, I think there's a mistake in the bill.
This isn't what I ordered — I had the risotto.
chunk_drills.spiralled_grammar: Hedging with 'Sorry, I think…' (recycled from the clarification chunk 'Sorry, could you say that again?'); /θ/ in 'think' + /ð/ in 'that's' back to back.

chunk_drills.label: Numbers at the table
chunk_drills.pattern: A table for ___. / ___ of these, please. / How much is ___?
examples: How much is the set menu?
chunk_drills.spiralled_grammar: Numbers and prices recycled; the three/tree and thirty/thirteen contrasts from the sound box are drilled inside real ordering turns.

guided_roleplay.learner_role: You are a customer arriving for dinner with one friend. You have a shellfish allergy and you want to pay for your own food.
flow: 1. Arrive and ask for a table: say how many people.
2. Ask for drinks and answer the 'sparkling or still?' question.
3. Order a main using 'I'd like the ___'.
4. Handle the news that your dish is sold out — ask what the server recommends and choose again.
5. Check ingredients and state your allergy clearly.
6. The wrong dish arrives: say so politely with 'Sorry, I think that's not mine.'
7. Ask for the bill and ask for separate bills; ask if you can pay by card.
sentence_frames: Sorry, I think that's not mine.
Sorry, could you say that again?

free_roleplay.ai_persona: A friendly, slightly rushed restaurant server on a busy Friday night. Warm, uses 'no worries', 'lovely', 'I'm afraid'; speaks at natural speed and checks back mid-meal. Never mocks errors; repeats or slows down once if the learner asks.
free_roleplay.a2_behavior: Stays on the standard script: seats the learner, takes a drink order, takes a food order, brings the food, brings the bill. Accepts short answers, offers a simple binary choice ('sparkling or still?'), and confirms the order back to the learner.
b1_curveballs: The dish the learner orders is sold out — the server offers two alternatives and the learner must choose and ask a question about one of them.
The server asks about allergies and dietary needs directly: 'Anything you can't eat?'
The wrong dish is delivered to the table and the learner must say so politely without apologising away the problem.
The server offers the special of the day at speed with a price ('the special's the sea bass, thirty-two fifty') and the learner must ask for a repeat or the price.
There's a service charge already on the bill and the server asks 'together or separate?' — the learner must query the extra line and ask to split.
The card machine is down: 'Sorry, cash only tonight' — the learner must cope and ask where the nearest ATM is.

roleplay_rubric.criterion: Ordered a main and a drink using 'I'd like…' / 'I'll have…' without switching to bare 'I want'
Asked at least one menu question ('What do you recommend?' / 'Does it have ___ in it?' / 'What's the special?')
Stated the allergy or dietary need clearly, naming the food ('I'm allergic to shellfish'), not vaguely
Asked for the bill and handled payment (separate bills / card or cash) to the end of the interaction
Used at least one clarification move when the server was fast or unclear ('Sorry, could you say that again?')
Stayed casual-polite: 'please', 'thanks', 'sorry' present; no commands ('Give me…'), no over-formality
Pronunciation: final consonants audible in 'rice', 'ice', 'bill', 'fish', 'peanuts'; 'th' clear in 'three', 'thanks', 'that's' — server never mishears the order or the number
Coped with an off-script curveball (sold out / wrong dish / cash only / extra charge) and repaired it politely without abandoning the conversation

register_culture_note.en: Restaurant English is casual-polite. The politeness is carried by 'please', 'thanks', 'sorry' and by 'I'd like' / 'Could I have' — not by long formal sentences. Servers are peers doing a job: you don't need to be deferential, but you also don't give commands. You get the server's attention with eye contact and a small raised hand plus 'Excuse me', not by calling out or clicking fingers. Saying there's a problem is normal and expected: 'Sorry, I think that's not mine' fixes it in one turn, and no one loses face.

do_dont.prefer: I'd like the fried rice, please.
'fried rice' with the /d/ and /s/ both landing — otherwise the server writes down the wrong dish
'three coffees' — 'tree' is heard as a count of one, or as nothing, and you get the wrong number on the bill

do_dont.avoid: Waiter! / clicking fingers / calling across the room
do_dont.prefer: Excuse me — when you have a minute?
Could we get the bill, please?

do_dont.avoid: Saying nothing when the wrong dish arrives and eating it
do_dont.prefer: Sorry, I think that's not mine — I ordered the risotto.
'no ice' — say the /s/, or your drink arrives full of ice

register_culture_note.thai_cultural_note: Two habits from eating out in Thailand don't transfer. First, ordering is usually individual, not communal: each person picks their own main and the plates are not automatically shared, so 'What are we all having?' isn't the default question — you order for yourself. Second, splitting the bill by what each person ate is completely normal and asking for separate bills is a routine request, not a loss of face; the Thai pattern where the most senior or the inviting person quietly pays for everyone is not assumed. And when something is wrong with the order, saying so immediately is treated as helpful, not as making trouble — staff would rather fix it than have you eat food you didn't want.

can_do_checkpoints.statement: I can ask for a table, say how many people, and order a drink.
I can order food with 'I'd like…' and ask 'What do you recommend?'
I can ask for the bill and ask if I can pay by card.
I can check ingredients, state an allergy clearly, and choose again when my dish is sold out.
I can politely say the wrong dish or the wrong amount has arrived, and get it fixed.
I can ask for separate bills and query an extra charge on the bill.
My final consonants ('rice', 'ice', 'bill', 'fish') and my 'th' ('three', 'thanks', 'that's') are clear enough that the server takes my order right the first time.
